This study investigated the relationship between cholinergic denervation and the presence, overall severity, and development of hallucinations in Parkinson disease. papers.title: Integrative blood transcriptomics identifies U1-snRNP gene repression and miRNA-mRNA regulatory hubs in pre-clinical Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons and the accumulation of intraneuronal misfolded α-synuclein aggregates. Despite advances in understanding the underlying molecular mechanisms of PD, diagnosis still relies largely on clinical symptoms that appear relatively late in disease progression. To advance both the mechanistic understanding of PD and the development of new diagnostic tools, we here performed an integrative analysis of matched whole-blood mRNA-seq and miRNA-seq data from 2604 participants (Healthy n = 658; PD n = 1946) of the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), stratified into pre-clinical (n = 561), mild, moderate, and severe stages. Differential expression (adjusted p < 0.05; |fold change|> 0.58) revealed maximal alterations in pre-clinical (7386 differentially expressed genes; 156 differentially expressed miRNAs) and severe PD. Pre-clinical signatures were dominated by widespread downregulation, notably involving multiple U1 snRNA genes, indicating early repression of U1-snRNP spliceosomal components. Integration of predicted targets with Spearman anti-correlation identified 251 miRNA-mRNA pairs, driven by hub miRNAs including miR-34a-5p, miR-1299, miR-3120-5p, and miR-412-3p.Taken together, these findings highlight the importance of early spliceosomal dysfunction and miRNA dysregulation in preclinical PD, supporting their potential as novel blood-based biomarkers.

papers.title: Sex and genotype influence the disruption of circulating NMDAR-related amino acids in patients with Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Sex and genetic factors influence the epidemiology and clinical features of Parkinson's disease (PD), but their impact on N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR)-related amino acids remains unclear. We measured serum levels of these molecules by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) in a well-characterized cohort of PD patients (n = 245) and healthy controls (HCs, n = 203), stratified by sex and disease subtype (idiopathic, n = 121; genetic, n = 124). The genetic subgroup included carriers of pathogenic variants in LRRK2, TMEM175, PARK2, PINK1, PARK7, and GBA1. We identified marked sex-dependent differences in amino acid profiles, confirmed by linear models with interaction terms. Idiopathic male patients showed reductions in serum levels of L-glutamate, L-glutamine, L-aspartate, D-serine, L-serine, glycine, and L-asparagine compared with HCs, whereas genetic PD males displayed more limited changes. Female patients showed minimal or no significant alterations regardless of subtype. Within the PD cohort, idiopathic males exhibited lower levels of L-glutamate, L-aspartate, glycine, D-serine, and L-serine than genetic PD males, while no differences emerged between female subgroups. These findings reveal a previously unrecognized sex- and genotype-dependent regulation of NMDAR-related amino acid homeostasis in PD, highlighting the importance of biological stratification for biomarker discovery and for developing targeted, personalized therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Plasma Metabolic Proteomics Links Phenoconversion and Disease-Specific Brain 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Pattern Expressions in Isolated REM Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cellular metabolic dysfunction has emerged as a key contributor to neurodegeneration, but its role in Lewy body disease (LBD), particularly during prodromal stages, remains unclear. We investigated targeted blood-based proteomic profiles related to metabolic pathways across the REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)-LBD continuum, and explored their potential as biomarkers of disease severity and phenoconversion. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, we enrolled 116 patients across the RBD-LBD continuum, including 47 with polysomnography-confirmed isolated RBD (iRBD), 45 with Parkinson's disease (PD) with RBD, and 24 with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) with RBD, along with 30 age-matched healthy controls. Plasma concentrations of 92 metabolism-related proteins were measured using a proximity extension assay. Motor function, neuropsychological assessments, and brain 18 RESULTS: Compared with controls, 16 differentially expressed metabolism-related proteins were identified across the RBD-LBD continuum, with predominant enrichment in neutrophil degranulation pathways. These protein alterations were mainly observed in patients with clinically manifest LBD, with DOPA decarboxylase demonstrating the most prominent differential expression and significant correlations with levodopa equivalent daily dose. In contrast, only N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was significantly upregulated in patients with iRBD. Elevated NT-proBNP levels were associated with orthostatic intolerance, increased PD- and DLB-related metabolic brain pattern expressions, and earlier phenoconversion. INTERPRETATION: Plasma metabolic proteins showed stage-specific alterations across the RBD-LBD continuum. NT-proBNP may have potential as a marker of short-term phenoconversion risk in iRBD. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: Multi-dimensional signal exploration on the effect of tremor interventions.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Machine learning in tremor time-series analysis has so far been applied to differentiate tremor disorders. Respective analytical approaches can similarly be geared to explore therapeutic interventions, which conventionally are assessed by their induced amplitude changes. This may overlook subtle signal alterations. Feature-based machine learning offers the potential to explore much more granular tremor signal changes induced by therapeutic interventions. OBJECTIVE: To investigate multidimensional time-series signal changes associated with tremor-modulating interventions, and to identify shared and distinct intervention-specific patterns across tremor conditions. METHODS: Sixty-six participants (Essential Tremor (ET): propranolol n RESULTS: Significant clinical and signal-based intervention effects were observed across cohorts with the strongest tremor suppression following DBS in ET and expected tremor enhancement following caffeine in ePT. While amplitude-related features decreased consistently after therapeutic interventions, dopaminergic treatment in PD was additionally associated with changes in frequency-related characteristics. Caffeine-induced tremor modulation formed a distinct multidimensional signal pattern, whereas therapeutic interventions showed partially overlapping effects. No single feature consistently characterized successful tremor modulation across all interventions. CONCLUSION: Feature-based ML reveals intervention-specific tremor patterns beyond conventional measures, supporting data-driven approaches for objective tremor characterization.

papers.title: Blood transcriptome change after deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Although deep brain stimulation (DBS) has been shown to improve both motor and non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) patients, the exact mechanism of action remains unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate changes in mRNA expression levels in PD patients after DBS compared to those before DBS. PD patients who were scheduled to undergo DBS were recruited from a single university hospital. Blood samples were collected before DBS and 3 months after DBS, and mRNA levels were analyzed using RNA sequencing. Across eight patient pairs, RNA sequencing identified 18 differentially expressed genes at 3 months after DBS (17 downregulated and 1 upregulated). Gene set enrichment analysis showed that these changes were dominated by a coordinated reduction in gene sets related to cytoplasmic translation and the ribosome, oxidative phosphorylation and the respiratory chain, and neutrophil-associated inflammatory functions after DBS. This study suggests that DBS could influence a variety of molecular and cellular processes in PD, including translational, mitochondrial-bioenergetic, and inflammatory programs, providing insights into its potential mechanisms of action. Further larger-scale studies are needed to confirm these findings and fully elucidate the potential neuroprotective effect of DBS.

papers.title: The potential role and value of phosphorylated tau protein in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease: research progress.
papers.abstract: Research on the pathological mechanisms of PD has long focused on the aggregation of α-synuclein, but the role of phosphorylated tau (p-tau) protein in the onset, progression, and conversion to Parkinson's disease dementia has received increasing attention. Based on a systematic search of PubMed and Web of Science, this article reviews the physiological functions of tau protein and its neurotoxic effects after phosphorylation, and systematically summarizes the clinical and pathological evidence for p-tau at different clinical stages of PD (the prodromal stage characterized by rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder, the clinical stage dominated by motor symptoms, and the advanced stage accompanied by dementia). Crucially, we explicitly distinguish correlational human neuropathological observations from causal inference: the cascade relationship between amyloid β (Aβ) and tau pathology described in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is used only as an analogy, and the proposed "α-synuclein initiates, p-tau mediates toxicity" model for PD is presented as a hypothesis to be tested rather than as an established mechanism. By drawing on the cascade between Aβ and tau in AD, the potential timing and mechanisms of p-tau in the pathological process of PD are discussed. Furthermore, this article discusses new strategies for detecting p-tau through peripheral biomarkers such as skin biopsy to assist in the diagnosis and pathological staging of PD, while explicitly acknowledging that direct evidence for cutaneous p-tau in PD remains very limited and that current skin-biopsy data relate almost exclusively to α-synuclein; it then reviews the current status of p-tau pathology research in existing PD animal models, including the discrepancies between neurotoxin models and genuine human PD pathology, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for a comprehensive understanding of the complex pathological network of PD and the development of new therapeutic ta

papers.title: Aging impairs CX3CL1 neuroprotection in α-synuclein-induced Parkinson's disease pathology.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most prevalent movement disorder, is pathologically defined by the accumulation of α-synuclein (α-syn), loss of dopaminergic neuron and inflammation in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The neuronally expressed chemokine CX3CL1 (fractalkine, FKN), when delivered as the soluble form (sFKN) via AAV-mediated overexpression, protects dopamine neurons in several animal models of PD. Since aging is a major risk factor for PD, we examined the effects of sFKN overexpression in both young and aged PD models. To model PD, young (3-month) and aged (15-month) male F344 rats received unilateral intracranial injections of recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (rAAV9) encoding either human wild-type α-synuclein (α-syn) or green fluorescent protein (GFP). Motor performance was evaluated at baseline, 1 month, and 2 months post-injection. Behavioral deficits and neuropathological changes were compared across treatment and age groups. CX3CL1 involvement in PD-related neuroinflammation was assessed using immunohistochemistry and biochemical analyses and bulk RNA-seq was used to characterize transcriptomic changes. We found that sFKN rescued both motor deficits and dopaminergic neuron loss in young PD animals but not in aged animals. Analysis of the transcriptomics revealed age-dependent alterations in inflammatory, immune, and neurogenic signaling in response to sFKN treatment. In conclusion, while sFKN effectively ameliorates behavioral deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration in young PD animals, its protective effects are lost in aged animals. These findings emphasize the necessity of rigorous age-inclusive preclinical evaluation and suggest that targeting CX3CL1 signaling alone may be insufficient as a therapeutic strategy in age-related neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: The gut microbiome and brain inflammation in Parkinson's disease: mechanisms and therapies.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common chronic progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 10 million people worldwide. PD is increasingly understood to have peripheral origins in a substantial subset of patients, in whom microbiota dysbiosis precedes and facilitates central neurodegeneration via the gut-brain axis. Dysbiosis-associated depletion of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, enrichment of lipopolysaccharide-producing taxa, and loss of gut barrier integrity activate toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)/nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling, prime microglia towards a disease-linked phenotype, and promote the misfolding of α-synuclein and its propagation from the enteric to the central nervous system. Complement, activated by α-synuclein and shaped by the gut microbiota, further links dysbiosis to neurodegeneration. Beyond neuroinflammation, the gut microbiome modulates levodopa pharmacokinetics through bacterial tyrosine decarboxylase activity and interacts with catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors to alter drug bioavailability. Certain microbial metabolites, including the trimethylamine N-oxide to butyrate ratio and secondary bile acids, have emerged as candidate biomarkers. Cutaneous phosphorylated α-synuclein deposition and seeding amplification assays (SAA) are evaluated as minimally invasive peripheral biomarkers, along with epidemiological evidence linking prior antibiotic exposure and inflammatory bowel disease to PD risk. Emerging therapeutic strategies include SCFA supplementation, fecal microbiota transplantation, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists, and targeted probiotics. Microbiome-direct strategies may benefit patients with a gut-first PD subtype, suggested by prodromal constipation, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder, or cardiac sympathetic denervation, underscoring the need for subtype-stratified trial designs. In this review article, we highlight recent ev

papers.title: Neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease: from glial heterogeneity and gut-brain immune crosstalk to precision therapeutic strategies.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuronal loss, α-synuclein pathology, and a broad spectrum of motor and non-motor manifestations. Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognized as an important component of PD pathobiology; however, traditional frameworks have largely focused on canonical inflammatory pathways and simplified classifications of glial activation, which do not fully capture the spatial, temporal, and functional heterogeneity of immune responses in PD. Emerging evidence from single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, together with studies of peripheral immunity and the microbiota-gut-brain axis, indicates that PD-associated inflammation is dynamic, context dependent, and systemically integrated. In this review, we critically synthesize current evidence on microglial and astrocytic activation, bidirectional glial crosstalk, α-synuclein-inflammation feedback loops, and the selective vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons. We further discuss region- and disease-stage-dependent glial states, systemic immune and gut-brain interactions, and inflammation-associated microRNAs as potential links between peripheral and central inflammatory responses. Therapeutically, we evaluate conventional anti-inflammatory strategies alongside emerging RNA-based interventions and targeted delivery approaches. Particular attention is given to the persistent translational gap between robust preclinical efficacy and limited disease-modifying benefit in patients, including limitations related to disease models, therapeutic timing, biomarker availability, patient heterogeneity, and blood-brain barrier penetration. Collectively, current evidence supports a shift from broad suppression of inflammation toward biomarker-guided, disease-stage-specific, and cell- or pathway-selective immunomodulation in PD.

papers.title: Beyond neuroinflammation: α-synuclein as a molecular bridge and organizer of immune communication networks in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as involving not only α-synuclein aggregation and neuroinflammation, but also complex immune dysregulation that cannot be fully explained by individual inflammatory pathways. Here, we propose a communication network-based framework in which extracellular α-synuclein acts as a neuronal pathology-derived signal that initiates multicellular immune communication. Recent advances in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, together with ligand-receptor inference, provide new opportunities to reconstruct these networks by resolving disease-associated cellular states, spatial organization and intercellular signaling. This perspective shifts current models from isolated receptor activation toward network reorganization across the neuroimmune microenvironment. Importantly, this framework offers immunologists a roadmap to move beyond neuroinflammation as a black-box endpoint, toward mechanistic understanding of how immune recognition of neuron-derived signals reorganizes tissue-level communication architecture. Accordingly, future therapies may benefit from targeting disease-associated communication networks in a stage- and context-dependent manner rather than broadly suppressing neuroinflammation or individual pathways. We hypothesize that α-synuclein does more than trigger inflammation: by engaging different receptors on different cells, it may shape the wiring of the communication network itself-which signals are amplified, which are lost, and how the network changes over time. Treating α-synuclein as the starter of molecular immune communication networks is a feasible way to study the pathogenesis of PD and to develop specific therapeutic measures.

papers.title: Subtypes of Fatty Acidopathy in Parkinson's Disease: A Mechanistic and Precision Medicine Perspective.
papers.abstract: The conceptual evolution of Parkinson's disease (PD) from a protein-centric disorder to a metabolic disease has gained substantial momentum. While the lipidopathy framework encompasses dysregulation across all lipid classes, the emerging fatty acidopathy concept offers a mechanistically tractable refinement, focusing on fatty acid side-chain dyshomeostasis as a critical determinant of α-synuclein conformation and aggregation. This short review argues that fatty acidopathy is a mechanistically defined, conditionally applicable subset within the broader lipidopathy framework, with relevance that varies across PD subtypes. We examine the hierarchical relationship between these concepts, the evidence supporting fatty acidopathy in α-synuclein-driven PD, and the therapeutic implications of targeting upstream metabolic dysregulation. We critically discuss the translational challenges of current lipidomic approaches, including distinguishing disease-specific from state-specific metabolic signals, defining pathological trigger points, and validating biomarkers across diverse populations. We acknowledge that current evidence remains largely associative and that rigorous, stratified trial designs are required to bridge the preclinical-to-clinical gap. The fatty acidopathy framework offers a conceptual foundation for future subtype-specific therapeutic development in PD.

papers.title: Bile acid signaling in the gut-liver-brain axis: from pathogenesis to disease-modifying therapies in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: The identification of gastrointestinal prodromal symptoms decades prior to motor onset, combined with the Braak hypothesis of ascending neurodegeneration from the enteric nervous system, has repositioned the gut as a critical origin point in Parkinson's disease pathophysiology. Within this paradigm, gut microbiota-derived metabolites have emerged as key mediators of disease initiation and progression. Among these, bile acids constitute a particularly compelling mechanistic link, functioning not merely as lipid emulsifiers but as pleiotropic signaling molecules whose metabolic fate is governed by the gut microbiota and whose bioactive derivatives orchestrate systemic processes ranging from mitochondrial bioenergetics and immune homeostasis to neuronal survival. This review systematically integrates the triad of bile acid metabolism, gut microbiota ecology, and neurodegenerative mechanisms within the gut-liver-brain axis framework. We examine how intestinal dysbiosis disrupts enterohepatic bile acid homeostasis, generating a neurotoxic milieu characterized by accumulation of hydrophobic, pro-inflammatory secondary species alongside depletion of hydrophilic, neuroprotective counterparts. We further dissect how these compositional shifts propagate from gut to brain, converging on the core pathological hallmarks that define Parkinson's disease. Critically, we evaluate the translational trajectory of bile acid-targeted interventions, while addressing the pharmacokinetic barriers of oral bioavailability and blood-brain barrier penetration that currently limit clinical efficacy. By synthesizing preclinical mechanistic insights with emerging clinical biomarker and trial data, this review aims to establish the gut-liver-brain axis as an actionable therapeutic target for disease modification in Parkinson's disease and related synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Heat Shock Proteins in Parkinson's Disease: A Dynamic Continuum from Neuroprotection to Pathology.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, is pathologically defined by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and the abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn) into Lewy bodies, which spread from the nigrostriatal system to the olfactory bulb, lower brainstem, limbic regions, and ultimately the cerebral cortex. Heat shock proteins (HSPs) are a group of essential molecular chaperones maintaining proteostasis in this disease. However, their roles are far more complicated than previous researchers considered. This is not a simple dichotomy. We argue that HSPs are neither intrinsically protective nor pathogenic; instead, they exist on a dynamic continuum shaped by disease stage, ATP supply, and the integrity of the co-chaperone network. We propose that HSPs' functional shifts in PD may be stage-dependent: HSC70/HSP70-mediated compensatory clearance predominates in early phases, clearing misfolded/aggregated α-synuclein by inhibiting aggregation and promoting degradation to maintain protein homeostasis. In later stages of the disease, PD pathology leads to ATP depletion and co-chaperone network imbalance, shifting HSPs' function toward HSP90-driven pathogenic mechanisms. This framework moves HSPs from a binary classification to a dynamic, stage-sensitive model, with direct implications for trial design and therapeutic timing. However, a systematic overview dynamic role for HSPs remains lacking. Here, we synthesize evidence on both the protective and pathogenic roles of HSPs in PD, providing proposed ideas for a theoretical foundation for developing rational, HSP-targeted therapies.

papers.title: Pharmacological inhibition of SGK1 reprograms α-synuclein-induced neuroinflammation and protects dopaminergic neurons in a Parkinson's disease mouse model.
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a major contributor to Parkinson's disease (PD) progression and is closely associated with pathological α-SYNUCLEIN (α-SYN) accumulation. However, the signaling mechanisms linking α-SYN-induced inflammation to neurodegeneration remain poorly defined. Serum- and glucocorticoid-regulated kinase-1 (SGK1), a stress-responsive kinase involved in inflammatory and metabolic pathways, may represent a key molecular hub in PD. Here, we investigated the role of SGK1 in α-SYN-driven pathology and assessed the therapeutic potential of EMM-3.20, a novel SGK1 inhibitor. SGK1 expression was analyzed in lymphoblasts from PD patients, and the pharmacological profile of EMM-3.20 was characterized in vitro. Neuropreventive efficacy was evaluated in a mouse model of PD induced by unilateral AAV-mediated α-SYN overexpression, followed by transcriptomic and molecular analyses. SGK1 expression was increased in PD-derived lymphoblasts, indicating systemic dysregulation of this kinase. In vivo, α-SYN overexpression enhanced SGK1 activity in the ventral midbrain and induced broad transcriptional changes associated with inflammatory, stress, and immune responses. Treatment with EMM-3.20 normalized SGK1 activity, preserved dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra, and improved motor deficits. Transcriptomic analyses revealed marked suppression of α-SYN-induced inflammatory pathways, including inflammasome components, cytokine signaling, and NF-κB activation. SGK1 inhibition also attenuated oxidative and ferroptotic stress, restored NRF2-dependent antioxidant responses, and reduced lipid peroxidation. These findings identify SGK1 as a central regulator of α-SYN-driven neuroinflammation and provide the first evidence that pharmacological SGK1 inhibition with EMM-3.20 affords robust neuroprotection in vivo, supporting SGK1 as a promising disease-modifying target for PD.

papers.title: Low-intensity focused ultrasound for neuromodulation: mechanisms, parameters, and emerging clinical applications-a critical review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique that combines millimeter-scale spatial precision with access to cortical and deep targets - including the thalamus, basal ganglia, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens - that otherwise require invasive deep brain stimulation (DBS). METHODS: We conducted a narrative critical review of mechanistic, technical, and clinical LIFU literature from PubMed/MEDLINE, Europe PMC, Scopus, Web of Science and ClinicalTrials.gov (final search 30 June 2026), synthesizing in vitro MAIN FINDINGS: Proposed biophysical mechanisms include acoustic radiation force, cavitation, and thermomechanical coupling at neuronal membranes, engaging mechanosensitive ion channels and reshaping excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) balance via glutamatergic and GABAergic pathways; the direction of modulation and the physical-to-cellular chain remain incompletely resolved. Theta-burst TUS (tbTUS) induces NMDA-associated LTP-like motor-cortical plasticity lasting 30-60 min. Human studies in movement disorders (Parkinson's disease, essential tremor), treatment-resistant depression, anxiety, pain, Alzheimer's disease, and stroke report physiological and early clinical effects. Importantly, the physiological readouts most often reported - motor-evoked potentials, local field potentials, functional connectivity, and neurotransmitter levels - index target engagement and acute neural effects but do not, by themselves, establish meaningful or sustained clinical benefit. Key challenges include parameter heterogeneity, auditory confounds, inconsistent reporting, skull variability, and a paucity of adequately powered randomized controlled trials. CONCLUSION: LIFU is a promising but still largely investigational technology. ITRUSST consensus safety and reporting guidelines are beginning to standardize the field. Current clinical studies remain small, heterogeneous, and mostly short-term, supporting biological plausibility and ta

papers.title: Evaluation of perivascular diffusivity alterations in Parkinson's disease patients with mood-related symptoms using the diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space index.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have focused mainly on the relationship between perivascular diffusivity and motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease (PD). The relationship with non-motor symptoms, such as mood-related anxiety, depression and apathy, remains unclear. This study aimed to assess perivascular diffusivity in PD patients with mood symptoms using the diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index, and to identify which of its directional components account for any difference. Eighty-seven patients with PD and forty-three age- and sex-matched healthy controls were recruited. Anxiety, depression and apathy were quantified with the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale, the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and the Starkstein Apathy Scale, and patients were grouped according to the presence of each symptom. Within the PD cohort, Spearman correlation, partial correlation and multivariable linear regression were used to examine associations between the index and symptom scores. PD participants with anxiety, depression or apathy had lower ALPS indices than non-symptomatic PD patients and healthy controls, and the difference between the latter two groups was not significant. The index correlated negatively with all three symptom scores, but only apathy remained independently associated after adjustment for coexisting symptoms and clinical covariates. The reduction was accompanied by combined changes in the numerator and denominator diffusivities rather than by a change in a single directional component. Altered perivascular diffusion is therefore associated with mood-related symptoms in PD, and the index should be regarded as an exploratory, structure-dependent imaging marker rather than as a direct measure of glymphatic clearance.

papers.title: Direct-access model for dysphagia management in community-dwelling older adults: retrospective analysis of 120 patients.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Oropharyngeal dysphagia is a significant geriatric syndrome linked to severe clinical complications, yet community-dwelling older adults frequently normalize symptoms, leading to under-reporting and delayed care. While hospital-based management is highly protocolized, routine community screening remains low. This study evaluates a community-integrated service model designed as an alternative to traditional medical gatekeeping through public health literacy outreach and direct patient access. METHODS: A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted on the 120 unique patients (mean age 81.56 years; 44 males, 76 females) treated between May 2024 and July 2025 at a private teaching hospital in Hong Kong SAR, China. Participants were stratified by entry portal into a proactive, community-driven direct-access pathway (n = 95) or a traditional, physician-driven referral pathway (n = 25). Swallowing status and function were classified using the Functional Oral Intake Scale and the Functional Dysphagia Scale. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to compare clinical profiles and outcomes between the pathways. RESULTS: The direct-access cohort demonstrated substantial medical complexity, exhibiting high prevalence rates of stroke (24.2%), dementia (24.2%), and Parkinson's disease (12.6%), which were statistically indistinguishable from the Clinical-Referral cohort (p = 0.741) At baseline, only 19.2% of the overall cohort presented with normal swallowing function, while 71.7% required immediate texture modifications. Universal care was provided, with 100% of patient-caregiver dyads receiving specialized education, 94.2% receiving tailored diet specifications, and 56.7% undergoing individualized rehabilitation exercises. Following intervention, 20.8% of the total cohort were successfully discharged, and 12.5% were triaged to external medical specialties. CONCLUSIONS: A proactive community direct-access mo

papers.title: Adaptive Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson's Disease: Results and Learnings from a Consecutive, Real-World Cohort.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS)-automatically modulating amplitude based on local field potential (LFP) activity -is a promising alternative to continuous amplitude DBS delivery (cDBS). Data on its efficacy and safety in real-world conditions are scarce. OBJECTIVES: The aim of the study was to report on the initial experience with alpha-beta (8-30 Hz)-guided subthalamic nucleus (STN) aDBS in Parkinson's disease (PD) in a single-center cohort. METHODS: PD patients were consecutively enrolled after STN DBS surgery, had traditional cDBS programming postoperatively, and were systematically reviewed at 3 months (initial LFP-guided cDBS setup), 6 months (preadaptive setup), 7 months (aDBS initiation), 8-9 months (short-term visit), and 10-13 months (medium-term visit). Clinical, neurophysiological, and patient perception data were collected. RESULTS: Of 18 patients (34 hemispheres) who were switched to aDBS, 17 and 15 remained on aDBS at the short-term and medium-term time points, respectively. aDBS was comparable to cDBS in most outcomes, and better outcomes were observed on motor fluctuations (Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale [MDS-UPDRS] Part IV-1.5 points, P = 0.02) and quality of life (39-item Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire [PDQ-39] Summary Index-1.4 points, P = 0.01) compared to LFP-guided cDBS. After aDBS setup, an 80% patient-reported improvement was observed in symptoms persisting on cDBS (mainly gait problems, tremor, and dyskinesia). LFP peak frequency remained stable over time. CONCLUSIONS: aDBS was safe, feasible, preferred by patients, and clinically comparable to optimized cDBS for most outcomes in a consecutive, unblinded cohort, providing additional benefits on motor fluctuations and quality of life. A systematic approach in selecting the LFP band and thresholds pre-aDBS and programming settings post-aDBS is recommended.

papers.title: Impact of multimedia scenarios on students' perceptions and discussion tendencies in problem-based learning: a comparative study of three sequential cohorts among Japanese medical students.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: While textual cases are common in problem-based learning (PBL), students often find it difficult to fully understand patient conditions on the basis of text alone. In this study, multimedia and text-based PBL scenarios were compared with respect to students' perceived understanding of patient conditions and their consideration of differential diagnoses. METHODS: In this comparative study of three sequential cohorts, from 2021 to 2023, third-year medical students at Nihon University School of Medicine participated in PBL sessions featuring three diseases, namely, Parkinson's disease, lung cancer, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, using either text-based or multimedia scenarios. Multimedia elements included medical interview videos, auscultation sounds, and computed tomography (CT) imaging videos. A total of 123, 114, and 118 students were enrolled in 2021, 2022, and 2023, respectively. After each PBL session, the students completed a survey and submitted a report. The topics selected in these reports were analysed and categorized into the following three categories: symptoms, physical and diagnostic findings, and differential diagnoses. RESULTS: In the Parkinson's disease scenario, which entailed the presentation of visible symptoms such as tremors and gait abnormalities, 83% of the students reported that they could understand the patient's condition, significantly more than for lung cancer (58%) or hypersensitivity pneumonitis (53%). Introducing multimedia elements such as auscultation sounds and CT imaging videos was significantly associated with a higher proportion of students who selected differential-diagnosis topics in the lung cancer scenario (p < 0.05) and the hypersensitivity pneumonitis scenario (p < 0.01). Moreover, the addition of multimedia medical interviews appeared to be associated with different patterns of student responses according to disease characteristics, with greater perceived understanding observed for

papers.title: Exercise to Enhance Mitophagy in Parkinson's Disease - A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Mitophagy is a central mechanism in mitochondrial quality control and essential for neuronal health. It is impaired in Parkinson's disease (PD) and mutations of a number of genes associated with mitophagy cause familial PD. Recent advances in the development of novel treatment strategies for PD include phase I clinical trials for selective mitophagy enhancers. Next to pharmacological approaches, specific lifestyles, such as regular physical exercise, can promote mitophagy and thereby mitochondrial health and may be safer than pharmacological approaches and associated with many other health benefits. Here we explore, whether the well-known benefits of exercise for PD brain may be mediated by improved mitophagy. We put the potential benefits of mitophagy in the context of other exercise-induced, brain-health promoting mechanisms with relevance for PD and summarize the available literature investigating the role of mitophagy in therapeutic effects of exercise in models of PD. While the potential of exercise to promote mitophagy and brain health is well established, little direct evidence exists that implicates mitophagy as mediator of beneficial effects of exercise on PD symptoms and progression. Based on the identified knowledge gaps, we reflect on how this interaction may be studied in the future.

papers.title: Evaluation of Tremor Degree Using Triangulation Estimation for IMU Volumetric Method Based on Robust Mahalanobis Distance for Outlier Detection.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder whose core motor symptoms-tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity-severely impair patients' quality of life. Conventional clinical rating scales are inherently subjective and exhibit limited inter-rater reliability, underscoring the urgent need for objective and quantitative assessment tools. This article presents a novel proof-of-concept study that lays the foundation for objective tremor quantification based on inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals. The framework consists of three stages: first, a robust Mahalanobis distance algorithm based on the minimum covariance determinant (MCD) estimator eliminates multivariate outliers from raw IMU data; second, acceleration in the sensor coordinate system is converted to the geographic coordinate system via quaternion rotation, the gravitational component is removed, and 3D tremor trajectories are reconstructed using Simpson's numerical integration; third, Delaunay triangulation partitions the reconstructed point cloud, constructs pentahedral voxels, and calculates the enclosed volume, which serves as an intuitive metric for tremor energy and spatial activity range. The method was evaluated using a BWT61CL IMU sensor (sampling frequency 100 Hz) to collect hand tremor data from four PD rest tremor (RT) patients and four matched healthy control (HC) participants under standardized rest conditions. To assess the ability of the method to distinguish pathological tremor from physiological motion, the control group was expanded to include four Essential tremor (ET) patients. This revealed a measurable reduction in tremor volume post-treatment compared to baseline, consistent with the expected direction of clinical observations.
